extracted.intended_audience: card issuers, banks and credit unions, compliance officers, regulatory counsel, and policymakers reading Regulation Z/CFPB final rule
extracted.subtask_short: Regulation Z late and penalty fee limits
extracted.subtask_description: Final-rule amendments to 12 CFR part 1026 (Regulation Z) setting safe-harbor dollar limits and related rules for late and other penalty fees, definitions for 'Smaller Card Issuer', disclosure and periodic statement requirements, and regulatory analyses affecting small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor late fee for Larger Card Issuers ($8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as provided in paragraph (b)(1)(ii)(E), a card issuer may impose a fee for a late payment on an account if the dollar amount of the fee does not exceed $8.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB will not apply annual CPI adjustments to the $8 safe harbor amount for late fees at Larger Card Issuers; instead CFPB will monitor market and adjust the safe harbor as it determines appropriate based on trends in pre-charge-off collection costs and other factors. If an issuer experiences higher collection costs it may still use the cost analysis provision (§1026.52(b)(1)(i)) to justify higher late fees. The CFPB expects the $8 amount will be adjusted less frequently than current CPI-based annual adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor amounts for penalty fees other than late fees (and late fees for Smaller Card Issuers) ($32/$43)
rubrics_metrics.description: A card issuer may impose a fee for other types of violations of account terms if the dollar amount does not exceed $32, and $43 if the issuer previously imposed the $32 fee for the same-type violation during the same billing cycle or one of the next six billing cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These revised safe harbor threshold amounts ($32 and $43) apply to penalty fees other than late fees for all card issuers and to late fees imposed by Smaller Card Issuers. The amounts in paragraphs (b)(1)(ii)(A) and (B) will be adjusted annually by the Bureau to reflect changes in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). CFPB estimates small proportion of Smaller Card Issuers currently charging safe-harbor amounts; changes will increase fees for some cardholders by estimated percentages described in the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-analysis based fee determination (§1026.52(b)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Card issuers may determine a permissible fee amount based on a cost analysis of pre-charge-off collection costs under §1026.52(b)(1)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where safe harbor amounts exist, issuers retain the option to use the cost analysis provisions to recover higher costs. CFPB notes that if an issuer raises fees based on cost analysis, the consumer impact would be the same as if that fee were allowed otherwise. The cost-analysis path remains especially relevant if CPI-based adjustments would have differed from actual collection-cost trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual CPI adjustments (for $32/$43 amounts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amounts in paragraphs (b)(1)(ii)(A) and (B) ($32 and $43) will be adjusted annually by the Bureau to reflect changes in the Consumer Price Index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB declined to apply annual CPI adjustments to the $8 late fee safe harbor for Larger Card Issuers. CFPB explains that collection cost trends for Larger Card Issuers and CPI are not closely related, and thus future CFPB adjustments may differ from CPI effects. The illustration in the rule compares outcomes under continued CPI adjustments versus CFPB monitoring-based adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Smaller Card Issuer (§1026.52(b)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A card issuer is a 'Smaller Card Issuer' for purposes of paragraph (b)(1)(ii)(E) if the issuer together with its affiliates had fewer than one million open credit card accounts, as defined in §1026.58(b)(6), for the entire preceding calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliate means company that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with another company per Bank Holding Company Act. If an issuer had fewer than one million accounts in the preceding year but meets/exceeds that number in the current year, it will no longer be a Smaller Card Issuer 60 days after exceeding the threshold. The final rule incorporates the 'open account' definition from §1026.58(b)(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open credit card account definition (§1026.58(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'open account' or 'open credit card account' is a credit card account under an open-end consumer credit plan and either (i) the cardholder can obtain extensions of credit on the account, or (ii) there is an outstanding balance that has not been charged off. Temporarily suspended accounts (e.g., unauthorized use report) are considered open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition is used for determining whether a card issuer meets the one-million-account threshold for 'Smaller Card Issuer' status and for other Regulation Z purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 25%-of-minimum-payment late-fee limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB considered, but did not finalize, an amendment to limit late payment dollar amounts to 25 percent of the required minimum periodic payment (instead of up to 100%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB concluded benefits to consumers (more proportional fees when minimum payment is small) did not outweigh considerations about issuers' ability to recoup pre-charge-off collection costs when using an $8 safe harbor, and concerns about impacts to minimum balances due. Thus the 25% proposal was not adopted for Larger or Smaller Card Issuers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of mandatory 15-day courtesy period
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB considered, but did not adopt, an amendment that would prohibit late fees assessed within 15 calendar days after the payment due date (a mandatory courtesy period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB determined, absent additional evidence, that impacts to card issuers' costs and potential consumer confusion outweigh the benefits. CFPB acknowledged commenter-raised benefits (e.g., mailed payments) but noted issuer recoupment concerns and confusion as grounds for not finalizing the alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of eliminating safe harbors altogether for late fees
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB solicited comment on eliminating the safe harbor provisions for late fees so issuers could only impose late fees under cost-analysis provisions, but did not adopt this alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB decided that revoking the safe harbor without replacing it was not appropriate; instead the Bureau adopted an $8 safe harbor for Larger Card Issuers as better achieving its goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of applying $8 safe harbor to other penalty fees
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB considered applying the $8 safe harbor to other penalty fees (over-limit, returned-payment, declined access check fees) but did not adopt this alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule does not expand the $8 safe harbor beyond late fees for Larger Card Issuers; other penalty fees remain subject to the $32/$43 safe harbor amounts or cost analysis as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFA/SISNOSE certification for small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB certified that the final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities (no SISNOSE), and therefore an IRFA and SBREFA panel were not required for the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB's reasoning: credit card assets and revenues represent a small share of most small banks' and credit unions' total assets and revenue; nearly all small entities for RFA purposes will qualify as 'Smaller Card Issuers' and thus not be subject to the $8 safe harbor. CFPB responds to commenters who asserted the rule would have SISNOSE and who sought SBREFA consultation, explaining its data and conclusions. SBA definition: financial institutions with less than $850 million total assets are small for the period used in analysis (effective March 17, 2023).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of legal due date vs. courtesy periods (Periodic statement due date)
rubrics_metrics.description: A card issuer must disclose the due date according to the legal obligation between the parties (the contractual due date), and need not treat the end of an informal 'courtesy period' as the due date under §1026.7(b)(11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If law or contract restricts assessment of late fees until some days after the due date, the issuer must still disclose the contractual due date (e.g., disclose March 10 even if law forbids a fee before March 21). Consumers' rights under State law are unaffected; disclosure must reflect the legal due date, not the date after which a fee may be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment and disclosure when fee or rate is triggered by multiple events
rubrics_metrics.description: If a late fee or penalty rate is triggered after multiple events (e.g., two late payments in six months), the card issuer may, but is not required to, disclose the late payment and penalty rate each month. The disclosures must be included on any periodic statement for which a late payment could trigger the fee or rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a cardholder has one late payment, the disclosure must appear on each statement for the following five billing cycles because a second late payment within six months could trigger the fee/rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure when issuer imposes a range of late fees or rates
rubrics_metrics.description: A card issuer that imposes a range of late payment fees or rates may state the highest fee or rate along with an indication that lower fees or rates could be imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, the phrase 'up to $8' complies with the disclosure requirement when a range is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty rate disclosure when highest penalty rate already triggered
rubrics_metrics.description: If the highest penalty rate has previously been triggered on an account, the issuer may, but is not required to, delete the amount of the penalty rate and the warning that it may be imposed, or alternatively may modify language to indicate the penalty rate has been increased due to prior late payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is permissive: issuers have flexibility to remove or modify prior-warning language once the highest rate has been triggered, but are not mandated to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that due date be the same numerical day each month
rubrics_metrics.description: The due date must generally be the same numerical date each month (e.g., the 25th), though the last day of the month is permitted (it will vary numerically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A due date defined as the same relative date (e.g., 'third Tuesday') generally does not comply. Exceptions: last day of month permitted; billing-cycle adjustments described in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in due date rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A creditor may adjust a consumer's due date from time to time provided that the new due date will be the same numerical date each month on an ongoing basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: creditor may honor consumer request to change from the 20th to the 5th, or may change due date for operational reasons. See guidance on transitional billing cycles for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Billing cycles longer than one month: due date requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Billing cycles of two or three months are permitted provided that the due date for each billing cycle is on the same numerical date of the month (e.g., Jan 25, Mar 25, May 25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the 'same day each month' requirement in the context of multi-month billing cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of legal due date when creditor doesn't accept/receive mailed payments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the due date falls on a day the creditor does not accept or receive payments by mail and the creditor must treat a mailed payment received the next business day as timely under §1026.10(d), the creditor must nonetheless disclose the legal due date (not the date on which it will treat mailed payments as timely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if due date is July 4 (a day creditor doesn't accept mail), creditor must disclose July 4 as due date even though it will treat mailed payments received July 5 as timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25 percent limit during first year after account opening (heading and application)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 25 percent limit in §1026.52(a)(1) applies to fees that the card issuer charges to the account during the first year after account opening as well as to fees the issuer requires the consumer to pay through other means (e.g., payments from the consumer's asset account).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule applies to upfront issuance/availability fees assessed at account opening; the CFPB provides examples (e.g., an account opening fee of $120) to explain application. (Text continues in the rule with illustrative examples.)
